terms.grammar: verb, irregular (in + sum), with in and the ablative, or the dative
evidence: Ter. Eun. 59: In amōre haec omnia īnsunt vitia
Cic. N. D. 1.117: superstitiōnem … in quā inest timor inānis deōrum
terms.comment: Latin turns “X involves Y” round: in X inest Y, “in X there is Y”.

evidence: Ter. And. 189: Nunc hic diēs aliam vītam affert
terms.comment: Of what a thing brings with it: work, worry, risk.

evidence: Cic. N. D. 1.117: religiōnem, quae deōrum cultū piō continētur
terms.comment: In the passive with the ablative, “to consist in”.

evidence: Caes. BC 1.75: sinistrās sagīs involvunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically to wrap up or envelop, and figuratively sē litterīs involvere, to bury oneself in books (Cic. Fam. 9.20.3); it never means “to include” or “to entail”.

phrases.latin: In amōre haec omnia īnsunt vitia: injūriae, suspīciōnēs, inimīcitiae, indūtiae, bellum, pāx rūrsum.
phrases.english: Love involves all these troubles: wrongs, suspicions, quarrels, truces, war, then peace again.

phrases.latin: nōn modo superstitiōnem tollunt, in quā inest timor inānis deōrum, sed etiam religiōnem, quae deōrum cultū piō continētur
phrases.english: they do away not only with superstition, which involves an empty fear of the gods, but also with religion, which consists in the pious worship of the gods

sources: Lewis & Short: insum · Lewis & Short: affero · Lewis & Short: contineo · Lewis & Short: involvo
